content: Massage and aromatherapy massage are commonly employed as complementary therapies to alleviate symptoms associated with cancer. These therapies are often claimed to reduce pain, anxiety, depression, and stress, although some studies have failed to demonstrate these benefits. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of massage, with or without aromatherapy, on pain and other cancer-related symptoms. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted up to August 2015. The databases included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, PubMed Cancer Subset, SADCCT, and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving individuals of any age with cancer were included, with no restrictions on language. Comparisons were made between massage using carrier oil only versus no massage, massage with aromatherapy (carrier oil plus essential oils) versus no massage, and massage with aromatherapy versus massage without aromatherapy. The review included 19 studies (21 reports) with a total of 1,274 participants. Of these, 14 studies (16 reports) were included in a qualitative synthesis, and five studies were included in a quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis). Thirteen studies (14 reports, 596 participants) compared massage with no massage, six studies (seven reports, 561 participants) compared aromatherapy massage with no massage, and two studies (117 participants) compared massage with aromatherapy to massage without aromatherapy. The quality of evidence was deemed very low due to small sample sizes, high or unclear risks of bias, and limitations in study design. Adverse events, such as physical distress, rash, and general malaise, were reported in two studies, while the remaining 17 studies did not report adverse events. For the comparison of massage versus no massage, the evidence for pain and anxiety relief was of very low quality. One study (n = 72) showed that short-term pain, measured using the Present Pain Intensity-Visual Analogue Scale, was lower in the massage group compared to the no-massage group (mean difference [MD] -1.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.67 to -0.53). However, data on anxiety relief, measured using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory-State, showed no significant difference between the groups (three RCTs, n = 98, combined MD -5.36, 95% CI -16.06 to 5.34). A subgroup analysis for anxiety relief in children indicated a greater reduction in anxiety for the massage group compared to the no-massage group (one RCT, n = 30, MD -14.70, 95% CI -19.33 to -10.07), but the effect size was not considered clinically significant. No significant differences were observed for depression, mood disturbance, psychological distress, nausea, fatigue, physical symptom distress, or quality of life between the massage and no-massage groups. For the comparison of massage with aromatherapy versus no massage, the evidence for pain, anxiety, breast-related symptoms, and quality of life was also of very low quality. Some benefits were observed in the aromatherapy-massage group, but these were not considered clinically significant. Mediumand long-term pain relief was greater in the aromatherapy-massage group (medium-term: one RCT, n = 86, MD 5.30, 95% CI 1.52 to 9.08; long-term: one RCT, n = 86, MD 3.80, 95% CI 0.19 to 7.41). Anxiety relief was also greater in the aromatherapy-massage group (two RCTs, n = 253, combined MD -4.50, 95% CI -7.70 to -1.30). Long-term relief of breast-related symptoms in individuals with breast cancer was greater in the aromatherapy-massage group (one RCT, n = 86, MD -9.80, 95% CI -19.13 to -0.47). However, these results were not deemed clinically significant. Medium-term quality of life scores were lower (indicating better quality of life) in the aromatherapy-massage group compared to the no-massage group (one RCT, n = 30, MD -2.00, 95% CI -3.46 to -0.54). For the comparison of massage with aromatherapy versus massage without aromatherapy, the limited evidence available did not allow for a reliable assessment of the effects of adding aromatherapy to massage on pain relief, psychological symptoms (including anxiety and depression), physical symptom distress, or quality of life. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the clinical effectiveness of massage, with or without aromatherapy, for symptom relief in individuals with cancer. Most studies included in this review were small, had significant methodological limitations, and failed to report key outcomes. Future research on aromatherapy and massage should address these limitations to provide more reliable evidence.
